rows: [p. 78] [Margin: Solem caput et caudam Cometae una recta linea contineri.]
[p. 78] [Margin: That the Sun, the head and the tail of the Comet are contained by one straight line.]

Asphal. Hoc itaque certum habes, solem cum Cometae capite et cauda rectam perduxisse lineam, quod tibi constare negaverit Galilaeus, cum ad hoc ut recta linea comprehendi plura videantur, satis sit in eadem superficie cum oculo contineri. [p. 79] Hoc autem tibi negato vides quo tota fabrica ruat.

Asphal. This therefore you hold certain, that the sun with the head and tail of the Comet drew through [perduxisse] a straight line, which Galileo would deny to be established [constare] for you, since, for this — that more [things] be seen to be comprehended by a straight line — it is enough [for them] to be contained in the same surface [superficie] with the eye. [p. 79] But this being denied to you, you see whither the whole fabric [fabrica] falls.

Ereu. Ita est Asphali. Sed nos Astronomorum placitis inaedificare sat est. Galilaeum autem credo non universaliter dicere quasi velit hoc asserere quaecumque in eodem circulo sunt, ex necessitate in una linea recta apparere. Hoc enim manifeste falsum est, cum alia in ortu, alia in meridiano, alia in occasu stella in eadem cum oculo superficie consistant; procul tamen abest ut in una recta appareant.

Ereu. So it is, Asphalius. But for us it is enough to build upon [inaedificare] the decrees [placitis] of the Astronomers. Galileo, however, I believe does not speak universally, as if he wished to assert this, [that] whatever things are in the same circle of necessity appear in one straight line. For this is manifestly false, since one star at the rising, another at the meridian, another at the setting stand [consistant] in the same surface with the eye; yet it is far away that they appear in one straight [line].

Negativus est itaque vel particularis sensus dicti allegati. videlicet non requiri ut sint in recta linea quae esse apparent, sed modo sint in una superficie posse contingere ut in una recta appareant.

Negative therefore, or particular, is the sense of the saying alleged. namely, that it is not required that [the things] which appear to be [so] be in a straight line, but, provided [modo] they be in one surface, it can happen that they appear in one straight [line].

Hoc autem inde contingit quod in ingenti distantia ab oculo incomprehensa, quae inaequaliter distant, aequaliter distantia apparent, ut montes altiores vel nubes post humiliores collocati oculo iuncti esse apparent: Sic ergo luna cum apparet media duabus stellis, non propterea censenda est in eadem esse linea sed in eadem visuali superficie.

But this happens from this, that at a huge distance not comprehended [incomprehensa] by the eye, [things] which are unequally distant appear equally distant, as higher mountains or clouds placed behind lower [ones] appear to the eye to be joined: So therefore the moon, when it appears midway between [media] two stars, is not on that account to be reckoned to be in the same line, but in the same visual surface.

Nihilominus si vera est generatio Cometae quam explicuimus, et quam non posse non contingere interdum clarissimum mihi est, unicam esse lineam necessum est. Rursus caput et caudam [p. 80] in una esse linea (cum hanc ab illo non progredi nullum suspicandi argumentum videam) necesse est accipere; solis autem locus ex computatione habetur: quare in eadem linea triplicem hanc faciem existere ratione tenebitur, non experimento ex eo quod sic perpetuo spectentur.

Nonetheless, if the generation of the Comet which we have explicated is true, and which [generation] it is most clear to me cannot not happen sometimes, it is necessary [necessum] that the line be single [unicam]. Again, that the head and the tail [p. 80] are in one line (since I see no argument for suspecting that this does not proceed from that) it is necessary to accept; and the place of the sun is had from computation: wherefore that this threefold face [faciem] exists in the same line will be held by reason [ratione], not by experiment [experimento] from the fact that they are perpetually beheld so.
Tandem ipsa inimicitia caudae cum sole et semper in oppositum solis sese versantis, et sub capite quasi clypeo sese tegentis, arguit eam directa ipsius spicula sentire.

Finally the very enmity of the tail with the sun, [the tail] both always turning itself into the opposite of the sun and covering itself under the head as under a shield, argues [arguit] that it feels the direct little darts [spicula] of it [the sun].

Neque Fromondianum spectrum abludit, quid enim est quod cum sol non solum plaustrum respiceret, hoc solum trahebat colorem, nisi quod decolorati percolatione per caput radii, solaris plaustri contingeret liras; actionem autem luminis per rectas fieri non est cur inculcem.

Nor is the Fromondian spectre [spectrum] out of tune [abludit]; for what is it, that, when the sun regarded not only the Wain, this alone drew colour, unless that, by the percolation of the decoloured ray through the head, it touched the furrows [liras] of the solar Wain; but that the action of light is done through straight [lines] there is no reason why I should inculcate.
Andab. Licet ne etiam mihi aliquid ex teste tuo expiscari?
Andab. Is it permitted to me also to fish out something from your witness?
Ereu. Gratum feceris Andabata, siquid nos adiuveris.
Ereu. You will have done [a thing] pleasing, Andabata, if you shall have helped us in anything.

Andab. Quod itaque colligo ego hoc est, vel authorem tuum (quod pigritor accusare) mendacem esse, vel quod mage suspicor totam tuam de Cometis Commentationem male consutam: Si enim cauda capiti (quod constans est) conserta est, et fit iis radiis quibus transfixum est caput, ii autem tellurem radunt, habebimus Cometam terrestrem et [p. 81] luteum.

Andab. What therefore I gather is this: either that your author (which I am slow [pigritor] to accuse) is a liar, or, which I rather [mage] suspect, that your whole Commentation [Commentationem] on the Comets is badly stitched together: For if the tail is joined [conserta] to the head (which is constant), and is made by those rays by which the head is transfixed, and these graze [radunt] the earth [tellurem], we shall have a terrestrial and [p. 81] muddy [luteum] Comet.

Praeterea quale est caudam statariam capiti cursori appingere? Hoc autem necessum est. Cum enim Fromondus ibidem reflorescentem caudam noctu, ubi mane nimio sole marcescentem reliquerat, invenerit, fit stetisse caudam, caput vero quoniam solis observabat iter, fas est celeribus equis vectum credere. Et quod hinc sequitur, caput populis Orientalioribus calvitium ostentavisse. Ubi nunc ingeniosae tuae substructiones quibus Coelum attingebas?

Moreover, what sort [of thing] is it to paint on [appingere] a stationary [statariam] tail to a running [cursori] head? But this is necessary. For since Fromondus found the tail re-flowering by night in the same place where in the morning he had left it withering from too much sun, it comes about that the tail stood [still], but the head, since it observed the course of the sun, it is right [fas] to believe was carried by swift horses. And, what follows hence, that the head showed off baldness to the more Eastern peoples. Where now [are] your ingenious substructures by which you were reaching the Heaven?

Ereu. Acute obiecisti, et fidem authoris tecum ego salvam capio: Ipsa enim Cometam suum luto extrahet, cum primos afflatus non in horizonte ortivo, sed in plaustro quo lutum contemserit, sit conspicatus.

Ereu. Acutely you have objected, and I take the credit [fidem] of the author [as] safe with you: For it [the credit] itself will draw its Comet out of the mud, since he caught sight of the first breathings-upon [afflatus] not on the rising horizon, but in the Wain, whereby [quo] it scorned the mud.

Non itaque radii tellurem stringentes prius caudam notaverunt, quam materiam in coelis aptam incidissent. Male itaque suscepisti caudam capiti semper immediatam, cum ipse crevisse eam in occursum capitis a plaustro, orientem versus testetur.

Therefore the rays grazing [stringentes] the earth did not mark the tail before they had fallen upon apt matter in the heavens. Badly therefore you assumed [suscepisti] the tail always immediate to the head, since he himself testifies that it grew, to meet [in occursum] the head, from the Wain, toward the east.

Quod autem caudam pigritiae incusas, quodque caput suum destituerit, in aequivocum laberis. Unde enim habes quod non ubique parem materiam adeptus sit, unde praecursori suo syrma ornaret? Quod si fuerit, parem Orientalioribus quam Grudiis pompam iactaverit.

But in that you charge the tail with sloth, and that it forsook its head, you slip into an equivocal [aequivocum]. For whence have you that it did not everywhere obtain equal matter, whence it might adorn a train [syrma] for its forerunner [praecursori]? But if it [so] was, it will have flaunted to the more Eastern [peoples] a pomp equal as [quam] to the Grudii.
[Margin: Parallaxim {?etiam} in Cometis valere.]
[Margin: That Parallax is valid also in Comets.]

Andab. Habebam et ego quod obiicerem [p. 82] videlicet ex lege parallactica manifestum fieri Cometam illum libertinum, quem tu deprimis ultra Saturnum fugisse, cum ex distantissimis plagis sub iisdem stellis fixis visus sit. Sed loquela tua manifestum te facit, quod Galilaeus sis: et non expecto aliud a te quam legem parrallacticam in Cometis non valere.

Andab. I too had what I might object, [p. 82] namely that from the parallactic law it is made manifest that that libertine [libertinum] Comet, which you press down [deprimis], fled beyond Saturn, since from most distant regions [plagis] it was seen under the same fixed stars. But your speech makes you manifest, that you are a Galilean [Galilaeus]: and I expect nothing else from you than that the parallactic law is not valid in Comets.

Ereu. Iniquum facis, Andabata, si discipulum, si amatorem, si veneratorem Galilaei appellavisses, patienter tulissem. His enim omnibus nominibus credam ingenuos rerum coelestium sectatores ei esse debitores, me certe profiteor, sed tanta indigitatione honorari nec ambio, nec patior.

Ereu. You do [what is] unjust, Andabata; if you had called [me] a disciple, if a lover, if a venerator of Galileo, I would have borne [it] patiently. For under all these names [nominibus] I would believe the freeborn [ingenuos] followers of celestial things to be debtors to him, myself certainly I profess [to be one], but to be honoured with so great a name-invocation [indigitatione] I neither canvass [ambio] nor suffer.

Sed et ipsa tibi coniectura male cecidit: parallaxim enim in Cometa admittere mihi equidem necessarium videtur. Neque rationem interest referre cum eadem sit quam exposuimus, cum ambulationem Cometae in diversum solis a reflexione non proficisci contenderemus.

But also the conjecture itself has fallen out badly for you: for to admit parallax in the Comet seems to me indeed necessary. Nor is it of concern to report the reason [rationem], since it is the same which we set forth when we contended that the walking [ambulationem] of the Comet into the direction contrary [in diversum] to the sun did not proceed from reflexion.

Etsi non possim tibi concedere parallaxim usque ad octavam sphaeram Cometam ipsum evexisse. Cum ipse Fromondus ex ore Astronomiae principum hoc tantum afferat, eum parallaxim sortitum Lunae parallaxi minorem. Alii et nisi fallor ex iis quos tu citas solari maiorem diserte afferant.

Although I could not grant you that the parallax carried up the Comet itself as far as the eighth sphere. Since Fromondus himself, from the mouth of the princes of Astronomy, alleges only this, that it obtained [sortitum] a parallax smaller than the parallax of the Moon. Others, and, unless I am mistaken, [some] of those whom you cite, expressly allege [one] greater than the solar [parallax].
Quid ergo ad id testimonium quod allegas respondeo? seligendos esse te-[p. 83]stes in rebus Astronomicis, neque historicis narrationibus iusto plus fidei tribuendum.

What then do I answer to that testimony which you allege? That wit-[p. 83]nesses are to be selected in Astronomical matters, and that to historical narrations no more credit [fidei] than [is] just is to be attributed.

Immiscemus enim nos coelo docti, indoctique, experimentaque coniecto suscipientes leviter credimus, facile divulgamus et authoritate magni nominis munimus. Desideratur autem ad pleraque, experimenta et peritia artificis et instrumentorum exacta fabrica et utendi consuetudo.

For we mix ourselves into the heaven, learned and unlearned, and, taking up experiments [experimenta] by conjecture [coniecto], we lightly believe [them], easily divulge [them], and fortify [them] with the authority of a great name. But there is required for most [things], experiments, and the skill of the artificer, and the exact fabric of the instruments, and the custom of using [them].

Debueras autem, Andabata, etiam loca ex quibus spectatus est Cometa, et stellas transparentes nominavisse: Occurrisset forsitan aliquid unde hos cum caeteris Astronomis in pacem et amicitiam reddidissemus. Nunc ut se res habet, non suppetit aliud quod regeram.

But you ought, Andabata, to have named also the places from which the Comet was beheld, and the stars shining through [transparentes]: Perhaps something would have occurred whence we might have restored these, with the other Astronomers, into peace and friendship. Now as the matter holds itself, nothing else is at hand which I might retort [regeram].
[Margin: An Cometae supra Planetas reperiantur.]
[Margin: Whether Comets are found above the Planets.]

Asphal. Quid enim tanti est Cometas Coelo donare, Ereuni? Nescio enim quid iam tum subodoratus sum, cum in ipso sermonis tui de materia Cometica exordio solem in toto regno Planetarum dominari dicebas. Quorsum haec restrictio? aut cur Cometae in Coelo collocari non possunt? si tamen non possunt?

Asphal. For what is [of] so much [account] in bestowing Comets on the Heaven, Ereunius? For I scented out I know not what already then, when in the very exordium of your discourse [sermonis] on the Cometic matter you said that the sun dominates in the whole realm of the Planets. Whither [tends] this restriction? or why can Comets not be placed in the Heaven? if indeed they cannot?

Ereu. Ego certe non renitor, nulla enim mihi oboritur suspicio, cur iis regnis non sint sui Cometae, et fortassis omnes illi quos hic novas stellas appellamus. Sed aliud est hoc inquirere an ibi sint et aliud an inde nobis appareant. Fortassis enim non possunt inde ad nos [p. 84] apparere, fortasse capite possunt, cauda non possunt, unde coelo fixarum attribuendi vel erunt vel non, secundum quod Cometae nomine aliud vel aliud accipimus.

Ereu. I certainly do not strive against [it], for no suspicion arises in me why those realms should not have their own Comets, and perhaps all those which here we call new stars. But it is one thing to inquire this, whether they are there, and another whether from there they appear to us. For perhaps they cannot from there [p. 84] appear to us, perhaps they can by the head, by the tail they cannot; whence they will either be or not be to be attributed to the heaven of the fixed [stars], according as by the name of Comet we take one thing or another.

Si enim Cometam vocamus a nostro sole in nubem impactum et ad nos restitutum lumen, sic nullos in coelo Cometas collocare securum sit. Si vero ab alio aliquo illuminante, quod sua sydera servent, reflexum ad nos per nubem lumen Cometam appellamus, sic in coelo etiam appareant Cometae, qui esse Cometae non appareant, detractis puta quas nobis iactent plumis.

For if we call a Comet light driven into a cloud by our sun and given back [restitutum] to us, so it would be secure to place no Comets in the heaven. But if we call a Comet light reflected to us through a cloud from some other illuminant, which their own stars keep [servent], so Comets would appear also in the heaven which would not appear to be Comets, the plumes, that is [puta], being stripped off which they might flaunt to us.

Ast ego cum ea quae notavisti verba promerem, satis habui me inter eos limites continere quos solari potentiae sine lite novimus patere: de incertis et iis quae non spectabant propositam quaestionem, tacere satius existimavi.

But I, when I brought out those words which you noted, held it enough to contain myself within those limits which we know without dispute [lite] to lie open to the solar power: concerning uncertain [things] and those which did not regard the proposed question, I judged it better to be silent.

Asphal. Nefas, Ereuni, atque ego mediusfidius me non tacuisse quantum qui pote plurimum gaudeo. Video enim mihi eventurum fuisse quod est in diverbio. Tacitas Amyclas perdidit silentium. Agendum itaque tibi est ut et nos certi simus solem nostrum non posse nobis Cometas Firmamento tenus ostendere.

Asphal. [That were] impious [Nefas], Ereunius, and I, so help me the god of faith [mediusfidius], rejoice as much as whoever most can that I was not silent. For I see that there would have befallen me what is in the proverb [diverbio]: Silence destroyed silent Amyclae. It is therefore to be done by you, that we too may be certain that our sun cannot show us Comets as far as the Firmament.
[End of Knot ix. Knot x begins on the same page (p. 84) with 'Ereu. Accipe igitur quid mediter', marked in the margin: Nodus X. Plura esse in universo per se lucentia.]
[End of Knot ix. Knot x begins on the same page (p. 84) with 'Ereu. Accept then what I meditate', margin: Knot X. That there are more [than one] things in the universe shining through themselves.]

terms: Optics: things in one plane through the eye may appear collinear; Galileo's point (Discorso delle comete / Il Saggiatore, 1619–23) against inferring the true alignment of Sun, head and tail.
be agreed, be certain; stand together
Here: Galileo would deny that it is established for you.
Cf. glossary 'superstruere = build upon'; bracketed to keep apart.
logical quality and quantity of a proposition
White reduces Galileo's claim to an 'O'-type particular, not a universal.
The eye cannot gauge very great distances; cf. 'comprehendere' in glossary.
Keeps White's contrast of demonstration and experience.
Sun, head and tail as one threefold aspect.
apparition, appearance (the 1618 comet as Fromondus saw it)
Pun on plaustrum = Wain/Plough: the light touches the Plough's 'furrows' (= its stars).
Light filtered and decoloured through the comet's head.
White's own word for the comet theory.
Possible pun (luteus = saffron-yellow); main sense 'of lutum, mud'.
Glossary 'statarius / excursor'; also comic: fabula stataria vs motoria.
A comet without tail = 'bald' (cf. 'decalvare', glossary); calvitium as rhetorical joke.
'Ipsa' (fem.) = fides: the author's credit rescues his own comet.
Glossary 'Syrma'; the head as the 'forerunner' of its own train.
Belgic tribe (Caesar, BG V.39), i.e. the Low Countries where Fromondus observed (Louvain).
Pun on Libertus Fromondus' first name: 'the comet of Libertus', and a runaway freedman that 'fled' beyond Saturn.
Ereunius sets the head low, near the Earth.
Distance by parallax (Tycho's argument that comets are supralunar).
loquela tua manifestum te facit … Galilaeus sis
your speech makes you manifest … that you are a Galilean
Biblical allusion: Matthew 26:73 (Vulgate 'loquela tua manifestum te facit'), the Galilean Peter betrayed by his accent; pun on Galileo.
From indigitare, invoking a god by his proper name (indigitamenta): to be called 'a Galilean' is too grand a title.
Earlier argument (part 1) on the comet's motion away from the Sun.
the sphere of the fixed stars
skill of the artificer / fabric of the instruments
White's critique of naive observation; cf. Galileo on telescope craft.
stars seen through the comet's tail
Observers' report of fixed stars visible through comets.
Here Coelum = the region beyond the planets.
Ereunius allows other illuminating bodies (other suns) for other star-regions; sense of 'servent' uncertain (keep / preserve / watch over).
Comets stripped of their tails ('plumes') would look like stars; cf. glossary 'barba / cauda / caput'.
wrong, not permitted by divine law
so help me the god of faith
as much as whoever most can
Classically 'diverbium' = spoken part of a play; here = saying.
Proverb: Amyclae, forbidden to report enemies' approach after false alarms, was taken in silence (Servius ad Aen. X.564; Erasmus, Adagia I.ix.2).
up to the sphere of fixed stars
notes: Unit: Dialogue I, Knot ix, part 2 (final part). PDF pp. 89–95 = printed pp. 78–84, from 'Asphal. Hoc itaque certum habes' (p. 78) to the end of Asphalius' speech '…Firmamento tenus ostendere.' (p. 84). Offset +11 holds (p. 84 = PDF 95). Knot x begins on p. 84 with 'Ereu. Accipe igitur quid mediter', margin 'Nodus X. Plura esse in universo per se lucentia.'

Readings: (a) p. 81 margin printed 'cuam', read as {?etiam} ('Parallaxim etiam in Cometis valere'). (b) p. 80 '…per caput radii, solaris plaustri contingeret liras': singular 'contingeret' with no expressed subject; 'radii' taken as genitive singular with 'percolatione'; 'solaris plaustri' (the Wain lit by the Sun?) uncertain in sense. (c) p. 82 'parrallacticam' (sic, beside 'parallactica' above) kept as printed. (d) p. 82 'deprimis' certain at 300 dpi. (e) p. 84 'quod sua sydera servent': sense uncertain. (f) p. 81 'parem … quam Grudiis': 'par … quam' irregular for 'par … ac'. (g) 'Galilęi' (p. 82) normalised to Galilaei. No illegible words.

Verification pass: Latin re-read against 150 dpi page images and 300 dpi zooms (p. 81 margin, p. 82 top lines); English checked sentence by sentence against the Latin. 4 corrections: (1) 'quae inaequaliter distant, aequaliter distantia apparent' — 'distantia' is neuter plural predicate ('appear equally distant'), not the noun; (2) 'Ipsa enim Cometam suum luto extrahet' — 'Ipsa' referred to 'fidem', not to the Comet; (3) 'possim' (p. 82) rendered potential 'could', not 'can'; (4) 'Cometae, qui esse Cometae non appareant' — both subjunctives kept potential ('would appear … would not appear').

Conventions as in glossary.md. Ampersand printed '&' rendered 'et' in the transcription. Spellings kept: authorem, caussa/caeteris, contemserit, sydera, Coelum/coelum (capitalisation as printed), necessum, mage.
